tabs.title: The Club Visit
tabs.description: Understand what Nina saw and learnt.

questions.q: Why is the asteroid belt not like a busy road?
choices: It has no objects moving around the Sun.
Most of its objects are satellites.
Its rocks are separated by a lot of empty space.
It exists only in photographs.
questions.explanation: The teacher explains that the asteroid belt contains a great deal of empty space.

questions.q: What did the students use their telescope to examine?
choices: The Moon and its craters.
The surface of Dimorphos.
A spacecraft flying near Jupiter.
A new asteroid close to the school.
questions.explanation: They could not see the small dark asteroids and instead observed the Moon.

questions.q: What made the DART film especially interesting to Nina?
choices: It proved that all asteroids would hit Earth.
It showed that a spacecraft could change a space rock's movement.
It explained why the Moon has rain.
It showed the first human flight to Mars.
questions.explanation: Nina finds it amazing that a spacecraft can give a space rock a small push.

questions.q: Why do astronomers observe a newly found object more than once?
choices: They want to make it brighter.
They need to discover its colour every day.
They want to turn it into a comet.
They need a better idea of its future path.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two says further observations help astronomers know where an object will go.

questions.q: Why are old marks on the Moon easier to see than similar marks on Earth?
choices: Earth's rocks are always softer.
The Moon has more telescopes.
The Moon has no wind or rain to wear them away.
All space rocks fall only on the Moon.
questions.explanation: Without weather, lunar craters remain visible for millions of years.

questions.q: What important difference does the teacher make about an asteroid near Earth?
choices: Being near does not mean it will hit us.
Near-Earth objects never orbit the Sun.
Nearby objects are bigger than all others.
Every object close to Earth is already dangerous.
questions.explanation: The teacher says a close approach is not the same as an impact.

questions.q: A friend says, 'The club did not see an asteroid, so the visit was useless.' What could Nina say?
choices: The telescope was too small to see the Moon.
Space rocks do not leave any marks.
The film was not about asteroids.
Seeing lunar craters also helped them understand space rocks.
questions.explanation: The Moon observation showed craters made by impacts, contributing to the lesson.

questions.q: A scientist sees a new object once. What should happen before a confident prediction?
choices: People should decide its name first.
The object should be watched on more occasions.
The club should take photos of Earth.
The scientist should stop using computers.
questions.explanation: Repeated observations make the orbit prediction more reliable.

questions.q: Why is a small change to an asteroid's orbit important for protecting Earth?
choices: It could help an object miss a dangerous future path.
It would stop the Sun from moving.
It would turn all asteroids into moons.
It would make every space rock much smaller.
questions.explanation: The DART test illustrates a possible small push as a form of planetary defence.

questions.q: What did Nina learn about staying safe from asteroids?
choices: People should stop looking through telescopes.
A movie gives scientists all the answers.
Observing possible hazards is a useful first step.
Spacecraft can remove every threat without study.
questions.explanation: The article ends by stressing that watching the sky starts the process of protecting Earth.
